Discharge Summary:  
The patient, a female with chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough with exertional dyspnea, was admitted with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis. Histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis, and treatment with oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation was initiated. The patient was discharged in stable condition. Key findings include elevated γ-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase levels, normocytic inflammatory anemia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and porto-systemic collateral circulation. Multinodular liver with fibrosis and focal atrophy were confirmed via abdominal CT and biopsy. Mediastinal and hilar adenopathy were noted, along with non-caseating granulomas. The patient’s ACE was raised to 201 UECA, and tuberculin testing and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative. Discharge instructions include continued prednisolone and warfarin therapy, follow-up with primary care and specialist providers, and monitoring for symptoms.

Chief Complaint: Profound hearing loss in the left ear, tinnitus, and dizziness  

Hospital Course:  
The patient was admitted in 2011 with profound hearing loss in the left ear and tinnitus. She reported dizziness, but no nystagmus was detected during physical examination. Tonal audiometry revealed a 37-dB hearing loss in the left ear with 70% speech discrimination, while the right ear showed normal pure tone audiometry. Radiological findings showed a left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) mass with a 4 mm diameter lesion encasing the left VIII cranial nerve. A key finding was a radiological correlation with a left CPA lipoma. The patient was followed up clinically and radiologically for two years without progression.  

Diagnosis: Left cerebellopontine angle (CPA) lipoma  

Discharge Instructions:  
The patient is advised to undergo routine follow-up with an otolaryngologist. Follow-up imaging (CT/MRI) will be scheduled as per the physician's prescription.

Discharge Summary:

The patient, a 57-year-old male with a history of extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) 3, was discharged following a successful mechanical cardiac support (LCAD) procedure for severe heart failure. The patient received LVAD support for three months, with mediastinal widening noted on a chest X-ray and CT scans revealing mediastinal lymphadenopathy without evidence of disease outside the chest. A pathologic mediastinoscopy was performed, revealing consistent SCLC. The patient was removed from active consideration for cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy was administered while hospitalized, with carboplatin and IV etoposide given. After his first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient chose not to continue it and worked up. Complications included cellulitis, neutropenic fevers with pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and prolonged nausea and vomiting. The treatment course was complicated, with renal function remaining normal, but signs of worsening overload with pleural effusion and peripheral edema developed. The patient elected hospice care and was discharged home, with the patient passing away approximately six months after chemotherapy administration.

Patient: [Patient Name], 72 years, Female, admitted for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Adjuvant systemic therapy with nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor anastrozole (Arimidex®) and CDK 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenio®) was administered as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Adjuvant 3D conformal radiotherapy was performed on the right breast and supraclavicular region.  

Following radiation, the patient developed moderate acute radiodermatitis with small moist epitheliolysis in the submammary fold. At completion of RTX, a 2cm wide circumscribed cutis edema at the irradiated area was noted, which later extended to cover the entire irradiated field, with inflammatory infiltrate, hyperpigmentation, induration, and loss of breast volume. A targeted punch biopsy was performed to rule out lymphangiosis carcinomatosa cutis. Histology confirmed no malignant tumor, but dermal fibrosis with thickened dermis and fibrosis extending into underlying tissue was present, along with panniculitis and chronic perivascular inflammation.  

The patient was diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months post-RTX. She declined systemic immune suppression and opted for topical steroids and lymph drainage at a specialized center. The clinical condition remains stable.  

Follow-up instructions: Schedule checkups, monitor affected areas, avoid sun exposure, and apply sunscreen. Discharged with a follow-up care plan. Informed consent provided for follow-up treatment.

The patient, a 57-year-old female with a history of epilepsy, haemolysis, low platelets, proteinuria, and renal failure, was admitted following a post-kidney transplant evaluation. Key findings included IgA nephropathy, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease. A kidney biopsy revealed a mutation at position 3243A>G, leading to heteroplasmy in leucocytes. The patient underwent a kidney transplant from a donor at 52. Two years post-transplant, she developed severe left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, which remained stable. Four years post-transplant, m.3243A>G mutation was detected with a heteroplasmy level of 6%. Discharge diagnosis included IgA nephropathy, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease. The patient is currently stable with mild microalbuminuria, receiving prednisone and tacrolimus, and recommended follow-up with her nephrologist.

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to multiple cervicofacial lacerations caused by a broken beer bottle. Upon admission, the patient was diagnosed with a suspected vascular injury in the neck zone II, confirmed via CT angiography showing contrast leakage in the right internal carotid artery. An angiography via the right femoral artery revealed extravasation of contrast media in the neck zone III. A stent was inserted at the laceration site to prevent further leakage, and the patient underwent surgery to remove the hematoma and assess for any other injuries. Post-surgery, follow-up angiography confirmed no further leakage. The patient's condition improved, and follow-up observation and antiplatelet medication were prescribed. The patient has been discharged and advised to continue the medication and attend outpatient follow-up appointments.

Hospital Course: The 29-year-old white male farmer was admitted with left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. On initial examination, splenomegaly was detected, and a high leukocyte count, low hemoglobin level, and high platelet count were noted. Laboratory analysis confirmed CML in chronic phase, and the patient was initiated on hydroxyurea, which was later substituted with imatinib.  

The patient experienced slow progression of splenomegaly until regression occurred within 3 months of imatinib therapy. Initial reevaluation at 3 months showed no symptoms and weight gain, but imatinib was discontinued due to pancytopenia. Bone marrow studies revealed complete remission of CML and numerous Leishmania amastigotes in macrophages. Treatment with pentavalent antimonials was initiated to address leishmaniasis, and the patient achieved complete recovery after 60 days of therapy.  

The patient resumed TKI therapy after acute cardiac toxicity was managed with amphotericin B. A final PCR confirmed deep molecular response. The patient was discharged with good health and recommended for follow-up care.  

Diagnosis: CML in chronic phase, pancytopenia, leishmaniasis, acute cardiac toxicity.

Patient Information:  
A 46-year-old male was admitted with B-symptoms, recurrent pneumonia, and lymphadenopathy. A CT scan showed enlarged liver and spleen, and lymph nodes (mediastinal and inguinal). He was diagnosed with CD hyaline vascular type and treated with six cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy.

After the fourth cycle, a follow-up CT revealed right pulmonary artery dilation with wall thickening and enlargement of hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes. Hemoptysis and erythema nodosum lesions were noted after the fifth cycle, diagnosed as Behcet’s Disease. He was started on hydrocortisone, azathioprine, and enoxaparin.  

Discharge Diagnosis: Behcet’s Disease with a pulmonary aneurysm.  

Follow-up: The patient is scheduled for a rheumatology outpatient follow-up.  

Brief Comment: This discharge summary outlines the patient's treatment for Behcet’s Disease and confirms the diagnosis, with a plan for ongoing follow-up.

The patient presented with burning, itching, pain, stinging, lacrimation, and decreased vision in her left eye. She reported sand splash to her eyes at the seaside three months prior and discontinued contact lens use ten days before admission. A canthamoeba sp. cyst was identified in the corneal scraping sample, which was inoculated for testing. At the second month visit, no growth was observed after inoculation of the corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plated NNA agar. The corneal scraping specimen was defined as "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis. The patient's case was approved by the Ethics Committee at Uludag University Faculty of Medicine (2016-9/18), and informed consent was obtained from the patient.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient [redacted] was admitted with an eight-month history of generalized fatigue, increased thirst, urinary frequency, reduced nocturnal erections, sexual desire, weight loss, and dry skin. The patient was diagnosed with pituitary germinoma and central diabetes insipidus. A physical examination and initial laboratory findings revealed hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia. An MRI showed a right-sided pituitary microadenoma, and treatment was initiated with hydrocortisone and levothyroxine. Follow-up studies confirmed the diagnosis and ruled out autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Tumor markers were negative, and a water deprivation test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. The patient was prescribed testosterone, desmopressin, and a tissue biopsy confirmed an intrasellar pituitary germinoma. A lumbar MRI and lumbar puncture were negative for metastasis. The patient was treated with whole ventricle radiation and showed improvement. Follow-up is scheduled for endocrinology clinic to monitor treatment and assess symptoms. Patients with intrasellar germinomas have a favorable prognosis and long-term follow-up is important to detect recurrence or disease progression.

Discharge Summary:  

The patient, a male with a 62-year-old age, was admitted due to early symptoms of memory decline and cognitive impairment. No prior neurological history or family history of dementia was reported, and no brain injury history was noted. His cognitive function deteriorated over five years, leading to difficulties in daily living and work. Cognitive impairment and AD-like hypometabolic pattern were confirmed via MMSE, MoCA-B, CDR, and global deterioration scale assessments. Cerebrospinal fluid tau, ptau, and Aβ1-42 levels were abnormal. A distinctively positive [C-11] Pittsburg compound B PET scan and [F-18] fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan with a typical AD-like hypometabolic pattern were also observed.  

Diagnosis: Alzheimer's disease.  

Treatment: Not included.  

Condition at discharge: Stable.  

Plan of care: Family is advised to follow up with a primary care provider for ongoing monitoring and management. Care and support services are recommended to assist with daily activities.  

Follow-up: Follow-up with a primary care provider for continued management.

Discharge Summary: A 19-year-old female patient with a history of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma was admitted due to occupying lesions in the right lung and pancreas. She was diagnosed with combined pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, including tumors in the left adrenal and paraganglion regions. The patient exhibited symptoms of fever, headache, and high blood pressure, along with findings of occupying lesions in the right lung and pancreas. The hospital course included routine follow-up and imaging studies confirming the diagnosis. Medical management involved treating symptoms and managing the disease. Discharge recommendations include continued monitoring for further treatment and follow-up.

A 17-year-old female patient, referred after 31 months of orthodontic treatment, presented with an unfavorable orthodontic outcome following surgical traction. Key findings include a space maintenance orthodontic device between teeth 12 and 14, with clinical exposure of the crown on the palate and three orthodontic buttons for elastic traction. Radiographic exams showed significant bone loss distal to 12 and mesial to 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within the ennis inverted Y. The patient opted for partial maxillary osteotomy on March 02, 2001, involving the removal of the right canine and a partial osteotomy. Post-surgery, elastic traction was applied to conclude the approximation, with intermaxillary immobilization for 21 days. A continuous arch was used to maintain stability and encourage callus formation. Full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 24, 2001, and the patient was followed up with removable retainers installed by October 23, 2001. The patient requested removal of the internal fixation on October 29, 2010, and clinical and radiographic follow-up confirmed stability and pulpar vitality after 10 years and 10 months of follow-up with excellent periodontal conditions.

The 87-year-old male was admitted to the emergency room with chest pain and light-headedness, which were exertional, left-sided, and pleuritic. He reported shortness of breath but denied infection. Physical examination revealed jugular venous distention and muffled heart sounds. The patient has a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, recent pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and nonischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction 35%. No further treatment information was provided.

Patient: [REDACTED], Female, 54, Discharge Date: [REDACTED]. Admitted with a sodium hydroxide splash injury to the left eye, resulting in light perception issues and conjunctival congestion. Initial findings included a diffuse corneal epithelial defect, stromal edema, and Descemet’s folds. The patient was treated with 1% dexamethasone, 1% atropine, and tobramycin. She was then prescribed prednisone 50mg daily for 10 days, tapering to 5mg every 15 days. Despite frequent use of topical steroids, a symblepharon and corneal neovascularization developed three months later. Subconjunctival bevacizumab injections (0.05ml, 1.25mg) were administered to the left eye, reducing neovascularization. Post-injection, she was advised to use 0.3% ofloxacin and 1% dexamethasone drops three times daily for one week. A second injection was given two weeks later to manage vascular perfusion. Visual acuity improved to 0.1 LogMAR two weeks post-injection, with corneal neovascularization reduced. The patient’s condition was well-controlled over the next months, and follow-up at 24 months showed no changes in VA or clinical status.

The patient, [REDACTED], was admitted with heart failure and renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The principal diagnosis at discharge was heart failure with renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The hospital course included symptoms of dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, and abdominal distension, with physical findings of irregular rhythm, hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Laboratory results showed elevated B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) levels and a transthoracic echocardiogram revealing right heart failure with dilated right atrium and ventricle. Further evaluation with ultrasound and CT angiogram confirmed a large renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The patient was deemed a poor surgical candidate and managed via endovascular occlusion, with the aneurysm completely obliterated and the feeding distal renal artery occluded. Symptoms improved, and ascites resolved. The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician, continue medications, adhere to a low-salt diet, and maintain a healthy lifestyle.

Patient Information: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male, diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV, and HIV coinfections, with Grade 1 oesophageal varices. Diagnosis confirmed in 1997, with vertical transmission. Liver biopsy confirmed cirrhosis. Complication: undetectable HBV-DNA and normal ALT values. Patient initiated lamivudine therapy in 1998, leading to undetectable HBV-DNA and normal ALT. In 1999, HBV-DNA undetectable by qualitative PCR. In 2000, lamivudine stopped due to relapse, HBV-DNA detected and viral breakthrough. In 2002, HBV-DNA detected again, leading to viral resistance mutations and initiation of adefovir. In 2003, adefovir and pegylated interferon were added, leading to ongoing resistance mutations. In 2004, HBV-DNA detected and tenofovir was started. Patient is currently listed for liver transplantation.

The patient, a 2-day old male newborn, was referred to us due to abnormal genitalia, imperforate anus, and distended bowel loops. Examination revealed a well-formed double penis with a normal urethra, left penis with proximal hypospadias, normal penile shaft, bifid scrotum, and a duplicated recto-sigmoid colon. The patient underwent laparotomy, colostomy, cystoplasty, and surgical exploration, leading to a diagnosis of abnormal genitalia with double penis and hypospadias, imperforate anus, and a duplicated recto-sigmoid colon. The patient was successfully discharged after a series of follow-up interventions, with instructions for regular care and follow-up appointments with the primary care physician.

Discharge Summary  

A 40-year-old female patient, [Name], with a history of ureteral stones, Behcet’s disease, and multiple myoma, was admitted for infertility treatment. She underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy. Timed intercourse was initiated three months post-surgery. The patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) based on irregular menstrual cycles and elevated anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels. Standard treatment guidelines in Japan were followed, with the patient receiving cyclofenil (600 mg/d) for 5 days, starting on cycle day 5 until 9, and chlormadinone acetate (4 mg/d) for 10 days. Follow-up with clomiphene citrate (50 mg/day) was administered starting on cycle day 5 until 9. A 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass was detected in the right ovary on the 11th day of the menstrual cycle, which was initially considered a follicle but was classified as a hyperovulatory corpus luteum (HOC). Subsequent mass sizes on days 16, 20, 21, and 28 were noted, indicating a gradual change in the mass configuration. The mass disappeared on the 62nd day since detection (19th day of the menstrual cycle), and it was diagnosed as a HOC. The patient was discharged in good health, with follow-up scheduled for her next routine visit.

Admitting Diagnosis: Paradoxical Reaction  
Hospital Course: The patient was referred to the department due to a new mass detected on chest CT during routine checkup. A CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy confirmed caseating granulomas, diagnosing paradoxical reaction. The patient was continued on isoniazid, rifapentine, and ethambutol therapy, which was adjusted due to liver damage. Symptoms improved, and the size of the new pulmonary mass was reduced. The patient is currently asymptomatic, and the original therapy continues.

A 22-year-old female of Indian origin was referred to the Department of Periodontics for persistent lip swelling and recurrent episodes of angular cheilitis. Hematological examination revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia with low serum iron and folate levels. Further blood investigations confirmed low serum iron and folate levels and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A biopsy was performed to rule out intestinal involvement, and Mantoux and Kveim tests ruled out active tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. The patient was diagnosed with oral Crohn's disease without intestinal involvement. Anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroid supplements were prescribed, with topical steroid applications advised for oral ulcerations and topical vitamin supplements for angular cheilitis. External gingivectomy was planned after extensive oral prophylaxis and subgingival scaling. The patient was followed up for 15 months, and no gastrointestinal symptoms were reported. Repeat hematological tests showed no significant changes from initial findings. Although the oral ulcerations and lip swelling improved, the gingival appearance did not fully recover. The diagnosis was confirmed as oral Crohn's disease without intestinal manifestations, and follow-up was initiated to monitor the condition.

Discharge Summary: 

Patient [REDACTED] was admitted to the hospital with difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain. During the physical exam, an external bulge was noted at the gastrostomy site, and there appeared to be external migration of the PEG tube. BBS was suspected based on these findings. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy was conducted to explore the issue, revealing a bulge at the fistula site with an internal bumper embedded within the gastric lumen. Following external traction, the buried PEG tube was removed without complications. A 14 F, 1.7-cm Mic-Key® button was placed over the guidewire successfully. Kidney, ureter, and bladder X-rays were performed, which showed no free air. The patient was discharged home without further hospital follow-up. 

Diagnosis: Difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain.  
Treatment: External traction, PEG tube removal, and placement of the Mic-Key button.  
Follow-up: Discharged without complications.

Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic pain syndrome with failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)

Hospital Course: The patient presented with a long-standing history of intractable chronic pain predominantly in the lower back and both legs, despite multiple surgical and non-surgical interventions, including 14 spinal surgeries, block injections, and medications. The patient was found to have a mixed pain syndrome composed of a neuropathic radicular component in both legs and a nociceptive component in the lower back secondary to FBSS. Initial treatment with spinal cord stimulation (SCS) achieved excellent bilateral pain relief for the legs but not for the axial lower back pain. Subsequent treatment with deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the periaqueductal gray (PVG) on the nondominant side resulted in excellent axial spinal pain relief. During follow-up, combined SCS/PVG neuromodulation systems maintained complete relief of pain in both legs and back, with electrode programming adjustments necessary after accidental exposure to magnetic fields or generator battery depletion. Wire-connector revisions were required after motor vehicle accidents. The patient's chronic pain condition was fully controlled with the neuromodulation intervention for the past 22 years, allowing him to return to a normal life without pain interference. Follow-up care includes regular reprogramming visits and maintenance of the neuromodulation systems. Signed, [insert name of physician]

A 76-year-old male presented with exertional dyspnea, visual disturbances, night sweats, and progressive fatigue. He had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus type 2, high cholesterol, and alcohol abuse. On physical examination, he exhibited petechiae and hematoma in lower extremities, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly detected. His white blood cell count was extremely elevated (220 × 10⁹/L), hemoglobin was low, and platelets were dangerously low. A peripheral blood smear showed a significant number of blasts and promyelocytes, indicating a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Other laboratory findings included elevated LDH and creatinine levels. The patient was treated with leukapheresis, chemotherapy, and ATRA, leading to improved clinical response and discharge with appropriate follow-up care.

A 67-year-old Hispanic male was admitted with generalized body weakness, difficulty sleeping, abdominal pain, increased thirst, and urinary frequency/constipation. He was diagnosed with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with squamous features suggestive of pancreaticobiliary origin. Chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine was initiated, but the patient had recurrent admissions with worsening symptoms and uncontrolled hypercalcemia. His course was further complicated by acute kidney injury, cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia, and pancreatitis, requiring percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC). The patient ultimately expired within three months of his diagnosis.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: Case 8, 30-year-old female  
Chief Complaint: Elevated CK, episodes of palpitation  

Hospital Course:  
The patient was admitted for further evaluation of elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels and episodes of palpitation. Initial ECG showed T wave inversion, and TTE was normal. Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous carrier status for a missense variant of unknown significance (VUS) in the COL6A1 gene (c. 1273-4T>C).  

The patient was monitored overnight and remained stable. Cardiology consultation recommended outpatient follow-up with ECG monitoring, Holter monitoring, and potential exercise stress testing. Discharge instructions included continued medication for systemic lupus erythematosus, follow-up with the primary care physician for CK elevation, and scheduling a cardiology appointment for palpitation monitoring. Genetic counseling was recommended to discuss the significance of the COL6A1 gene variant.  

Follow-up instructions include continued care for systemic lupus, follow-up with primary care, and cardiology monitoring. Orthopedic evaluation for myalgia was also recommended. The patient is discharged in stable condition with follow-up appointments.

Brief Hospital Course: A 29-year-old female medical microbiologist in training was admitted on [Redacted] with symptoms of low-grade fever, general malaise, and retro-orbital headache, which developed three days after returning from Suriname. She reported being bitten by mosquitoes during her visit to Paramaribo, Brokopondo Lake, and Commewijne. Summary of Events: The patient was diagnosed with ZIKV infection after returning from a trip to Suriname where she had been bitten by mosquitoes. She presented with fever, malaise, and eye-related symptoms, which were followed by a rash and swelling. She remained stable throughout her stay and was discharged after 7 days.

Follow-Up: Follow-up instructions were provided to the patient and to seek medical attention if any future concerns develop. Further management was deferred. The patient is discharged home in stable condition.

Patient, a 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse and newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer, was readmitted to the hospital with shortness of breath. He had been on chemotherapy and radiation for his lung cancer over the course of the previous month. Four days prior to this admission, he was diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis, which was treated with medication. The patient was started on intravenous ertapenem for purulent pericarditis.

Upon admission, the patient had a temperature and was slightly hypoxic. During the physical examination, he was found to have marked jugular venous distension without Kussmaul's sign and pulsus paradoxus. Laboratory results showed significant abnormalities, including reduced white blood cell and neutrophil counts, elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and high lactic acid levels. An electrocardiogram showed normal voltage with diffuse ST-segment elevations. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology and right ventricular collapse in diastole and dilated inferior vena cava. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed, and 800 mL of green fluid was drained.

The patient was discharged home on the eighth day of hospitalization. He underwent partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear despite an extensive work-up including a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and the chest. The patient was discharged 2 months after discharge and resumed chemo-radiation therapy 2 months after discharge. There was no recurrence of pericardial effusion according to the TTE 4 weeks following discharge.

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with recurrent abdominal pain in the left lumbar region for the past four years. A renal ultrasound revealed left hydronephrosis. The patient underwent various tests, including a renal ultrasound, which showed incomplete duplication of the right side with left hydronephrosis and hydroureter. During the try-in step, a gold crown for tooth 36 slid from the surgeon's hand and was found near the endotracheal tube balloon. The prosthesis was promptly removed using video-assisted laryngoscopy and curvilinear forceps. Dental floss-tied gauze packing was performed to prevent recurrence. No complications were reported, and the patient was discharged 1 hour after stabilization.

Physical examination revealed arterial blood pressure of 135/90 mmHg, heart rate of 110 beats per minute, SpO2 94% on room air, and respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. No significant medical history was noted. Diagnostic testing showed normal cardiac enzymes, biochemical analysis, and complete blood count, except for elevated eosinophilia. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly with bulging left heart border. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with poor progression of R waves in leads v4, v5, and v6 and no ST segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large multicystic mass intrapericardially extending from the left ventricle lateral wall to the pericardial sac, causing pressure on the left ventricle. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous multiple cardiac hydatid cyst with internal trabeculae arising from the pericardium. A serologic test for hydatidosis was positive, and the patient had marked eosinophilia. After surgery, the cyst was successfully removed, and postoperative pain was managed with bupivacain, tramadol, and diclofenac sodium. The patient was extubated and had a normal hemodynamic status. Follow-up was uneventful, and the patient was discharged with no restrictions. The patient was advised to follow up with her physician for further management.

A 70-year-old male with a fractured right femoral neck due to age-related osteoporosis was admitted following a fall at home. Radiographic findings confirmed a femoral neck fracture, and a posterior hemi-replacement arthroplasty was performed with a cemented bipolar prosthesis. Postoperatively, the patient experienced clicking in the right hip while walking.  

The patient was readmitted for follow-up and radiographs were performed, revealing no open wound, scar, or dilated veins. Palpation of the right Scarpa's area showed bitrochanteric compression test positive. No neurological deficits were noted. Radiographs showed dissociation of the components at the femoral head-neck junction.  

Open reduction was performed through the old surgical scar, with the femoral head component intraoperatively placed in the acetabulum and covered with a well-healed capsule. The tapered parts at the inner head and stem neck were intact. The extracted prosthesis was removed.  

Follow-up was performed for 1 year, and the patient is currently asymptomatic with a favorable outcome. A post-operative X-ray of the pelvis shows a new femoral head with a longer offset assembled to the old femoral stem.

The patient, a 61-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital for irritable cough without medical history of interest. Gene testing showed PD-L1 positivity (50%), tumor mutational burden (high), EGFR E19 mutation and MET amplification. The patient was treated with gefitinib 250mg QD and crizotinib BID, leading to partial remission (PR) in December 2017.

In April 2018, masses in the lung were larger than before, with EGFR and MET mutations confirmed. The patient was given gefitinib 250mg QD and crizotinib BID, resulting in further partial remission (PR) in June 2018. A genetic test was performed again, confirming PD-L1 positivity and tumor mutational burden. Salvage therapy included pembrolizumab 100mg IV every 21 days and pemetrexed 800mg IV + carboplatin 0.4g IV every 28 days for six cycles, followed by maintenance of pemetrexed. CT scans showed clinical response with shrinkage of over 30% of the lung lesion on February 27, 2019, and PR on June 26, 2019. The liver mass also decreased significantly.

Discharge Diagnosis: Stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with EGFR exon 19 deletion and MET amplification. Hospital Course Summary: The patient was diagnosed with stage IV NSCLC and received combination therapy, salvage therapy, and follow-up care to manage the disease effectively.

Admitting Diagnosis: Disproportionate enlargement of right lower limb, abdominal swelling, and growth retardation

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 18-year-old male undergraduate student, presented with a disproportionate enlargement of the right lower limb since the age of 10 years, abdominal swelling for the last 5 years, and growth retardation. He was the first issue from a non-consanguineous marriage and had a normal delivery and normal initial growth spurt that slowed down with adolescence. The patient underwent several evaluations, including physical examination, USG abdomen, and femoral angiography, to establish a diagnosis. Based on the clinical evaluation, the differential diagnosis included Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome, Proteus syndrome, Parkes Weber syndrome, Neurofibromatosis type 1, and Hemihyperplasia-multiple lipomatosis syndrome. Neurofibromatosis type 1 and Hemihyperplasia-multiple lipomatosis syndrome were ruled out due to the absence of stigmata of these diseases. Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome, Proteus syndrome, and Parkes Weber syndrome were considered, and the patient was eventually diagnosed with Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome based on the clinical presentations.

The patient had abnormal body habitus with kyphoscoliosis, left-sided gynecomastia, and gigantic overgrowth of the right lower limb, including toes. His left lower limb was comparatively atrophied. There were multiple nevi distributed predominantly over the right flank, buttock, and right leg with secondary edema, occasional exudation, and eczematous skin changes in the whole of the right lower limb. These epidermal nevi had a mosaic distribution without any cerebriform or gyriform malformation. He also had a huge splenomegaly (15 cm below the costal margin in its axis). The peripheral blood picture revealed trilineage suppression, though bone marrow study was normal. This could be explained by hypersplenism.

On the final evaluation, the patient was found to have only venous malformations with no arterial involvement. Parkes Weber syndrome was ruled out due to the absence of underlying arteriovenous shunts. Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome was diagnosed as a multicompartment anomaly presenting since birth, characterized by slow flow, mixed capillary venous and lymphatic malformations, and severely affecting the right lower limbs.

Underlying comorbidities, medications, and allergies were not reported in this episode of care.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with no further intervention required.

The patient was advised to undergo regular clinical evaluations to monitor his condition and for appropriate management.

The patient was provided with all available information regarding his condition and advised to follow a regular follow-up plan and continue to take good care of his health.

The patient is a 22-year-old male with non-seminomatous germinal tumor (NSGT) E-IB, diagnosed and treated with left inguinal orchiectomy, which revealed mixed germ cells including embryonal carcinoma, mature teratoma, and seminoma. He received two cycles of chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) and continued yearly follow-up with no evidence of relapse. Subcutaneous interferon β-1a was administered, and clinical evolution was favorable until AFP levels increased and a PET scan revealed increased uptake in the left supraclavicular region and both lungs.

The patient was then considered for intensive chemotherapy and autologous stem cell support but declined. An additional BOMP-EPI cycle was administered as consolidation. After three months, a cervical adenopathy was detected, confirmed via fine needle biopsy, and radiated to the left supraclavicular region. Radiotherapy (44 Gy) was administered, but the patient refused further treatment. He resumed gemcitabine therapy, which showed a good response initially, but progressive worsening was noted after follow-up CT scans. Taxol, ifosfamide, and carboplatin were administered with cisplatin substitution. Despite aggressive management, the patient experienced a progressive decline in health, resulting in his recent passing.  

Assessment and Plan: The patient had significant past medical history including NSGT-E1B and MS. Despite aggressive management, the patient experienced a progressive decline in health, leading to his recent passing. Follow-up will be at the discretion of the patient's family.

Patient Information: [Patient’s name], 38 years old, female. Diagnosis: Recurrent ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast. The patient underwent total mastectomy with immediate reconstruction using a DIEP flap due to her active running career and prior whole-breast irradiation. The patient elected to receive a DIEP flap reconstruction.

Procedure: A stacked DIEP flap was performed, utilizing both hemi-abdominal flaps. Two single perforators were selected for each hemi-abdomen and dissected to their respective deep inferior epigastric pedicles. One set of deep inferior epigastric vessels was anastomosed to the antegrade internal mammary vessels, and the other set was anastomosed to the retrograde internal mammary vessels. The flap was folded and inset in a stacked manner to ensure maximum volume and projection.

Outcomes: The patient achieved a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with a good size match, and no fat necrosis was observed. A chest CT angiogram was performed incidentally for respiratory concerns on postoperative day 5, revealing patent vascular anastomoses to both pedicles.

Follow-up: The patient was discharged with appropriate wound care and follow-up appointments. A one-year follow-up was conducted, and the patient reported a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with no complications.

Discharge Summary:  
A 9-month male patient with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) was admitted following 8 days of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, vomiting, and decreased oral intake. Initial laboratory findings included leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolysis, as well as findings of echogenic but normal-sized kidneys on abdominal ultrasound. Peritoneal dialysis was initiated due to lack of response to intravenous furosemide. Stool studies confirmed Norovirus GI/GII as the cause of infection, and laboratory results showed massive albuminuria and low complement levels. The patient received one unit of packed red blood cells and continued peritoneal dialysis for five days. By the 10th day, kidney function and albuminuria normalized, and C3 and C4 complement levels returned to normal after three weeks. The patient was followed for 11 months, with no signs of residual damage, normotension, and no microalbuminuria. Parents were advised to continue with pediatrician visits and a healthy lifestyle. No follow-up testing was mentioned in the case report.

An 85-year-old Japanese woman with Stage IV squamous cell lung cancer was admitted with rapidly worsening general fatigue and appetite loss eight days after receiving the eighth cycle of pembrolizumab. She had been diagnosed with Stage IV cancer seven months prior. Pembrolizumab was the first-line therapy, resulting in stable disease. Routine examination before each infusion showed no significant changes up to the eighth cycle.

Physical examination revealed no notable findings in head, neck, chest, abdomen, or extremities. No visual deficit was apparent according to the confrontation method.

Laboratory findings included a low serum cortisol level, an inappropriately low ACTH level, hyponatremia with a raised antidiuretic hormone (ADH), and hypoglycemia. Urine osmolarity was elevated despite low plasma osmolarity, indicating inappropriate ADH secretion. There was a poor response to standard-dose short ACTH testing. Serum anti-pituitary cell antibody-1 was negative.

The patient was diagnosed with isolated ACTH deficiency. Hydrocortisone was administered swiftly, which improved her general condition, normalized the ADH level, and corrected the hyponatremia. Adrenal glands were unremarkable on CT. She was discharged and followed monthly in outpatient care. Follow-up showed that cortisol levels ranged from 8.12 to 18.3 μg/dL, while ACTH levels were not detectable during the observation period. ACTH deficiency remained, with no significant changes in thyroid function or other parameters. White blood cell, eosinophil, and electrolyte levels were unremarkable.

Admission Diagnosis: Epigastric pain, vomiting  
Discharge Diagnosis: Symptomatic cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland  

The patient was admitted with persistent epigastric pain and vomiting, which were not related to food intake. An ultrasonography and CT scan were performed, revealing a cystic-like retroperitoneal mass on the left side. Due to persistent pain, a CT-guided puncture was performed, but the cyst was not completely evacuated. Cytology was negative for malignant cells and compatible with a cystic lymphangioma.  

To assess the location of the cyst more precisely, the patient underwent an MRI. T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MR-sequences showed a lesion compatible with a cystic lymphangioma. Due to ongoing symptoms, a surgical resection of this cystic lesion was proposed. The tumor was confirmed to originate from the left adrenal gland, and an "en bloc" left adrenalectomy was performed without rupture. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5.  

Follow-up: The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic one month after the surgery and reported no further symptoms. Histopathology confirmed the final diagnosis of cystic lymphangioma.  

Differential Diagnosis: Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts were considered.  

Treatment: Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for symptomatic cystic lymphangioma. Complete resection of the cyst is recommended, and associated parenchymal resection (adrenalectomy) depends on the location of the cyst and intraoperative dissection.  

Discharge Condition: The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up as an outpatient.  

Follow-up Plan: The patient was advised to return to the outpatient clinic for follow-up consultations.

A middle ear inspection and ossicular reconstruction on the left side were performed due to conductive hearing loss and difficulty in wearing hearing aids with glasses. CT scans preoperatively showed epitympanic ossicular fixation and a more horizontal orientation of the incus and dehiscent facial nerve canal on the left side. Curetting of the epitympanic fixation of the malleus, removal of the anteriorly fixed manubrium, and repositioning of the ossicular chain resulted in a mobile ossicular chain. Although the empyema cavity was reducing, infection persisted. On postoperative day 36, non-open wound therapy with Negative Pressure Wound Therapy with instillation (NPWTi-d) was initiated. The patient received this treatment continuously for 20 days until the empyema was resolved. Four months later, no empyema recurrence was observed, and the patient was discharged with follow-up care. Discharge Summary:  
A five-year-old female cousin of Case-2 presents with minimal skin lesions and abnormal gait, but normal intelligence. An additional radiographic study was performed, revealing abnormal craniofacial contours in two children with severe idiopathic spondyloepiphyseal (ISH) disease. Case-1 displayed brachycephaly and partial closure of coronal and lambdoid processes, while Case-2 showed scaphocephaly with sagittal suture synostosis. A 3D CT scan of Case-2 showed total synostosis of the sagittal suture with mild plagiocephaly, and AP radiographs of Case-1 showed severe osteolysis in the shoulders and hips, with multiple dislocations secondary to massive osteolysis. Case-4's AP pelvis radiograph showed "shepherd's crook" deformity with coxa vara, and Case-5's AP pelvis radiograph displayed a less important malformation complex. The patient's skeletal phenotype is characterized by abnormal craniofacial contours, severe osteolysis, and deformed pelvis. Follow-up radiographic studies and further evaluation are recommended.

In conclusion, the patient had a history of multiple medical conditions and presented with neurological symptoms. After a brain biopsy, he was diagnosed with necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis and received various treatments, but the disease progressed to a point of death.

She was discharged with a partial response as per RECIST, and imaging resolved periaortic nodules and liver metastases. Nontarget lesions in the left eighth rib and brain remained stable. A 45-year-old woman referred to the hospital for systemic symptoms including fever, weight loss, and general malaise was found to have multiple small violaceous plaques on her skin. Upon admission, she exhibited low-grade fever, weight loss, and increased lymph node size. A skin biopsy confirmed infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, with immunohistochemical studies excluding malignant lymphoma. The patient was discharged with no further treatment and scheduled for follow-up with the dermatology department. Her condition is currently classified as a systemic disorder, and further diagnostic testing is recommended to determine the underlying cause. The patient is advised to continue prescribed medications and attend follow-up appointments. The prognosis remains uncertain at this time.

The patient, a 35-year-old male, was admitted with multiple abrasions over the right thigh, a lacerated wound over the right hand, and a deep perforated wound of the right eye, likely caused by a tangentially flying foreign body. A primary survey and brief history were conducted to assess the injury sequence and mode of injury. After initial resuscitation and sterilization, the patient underwent a CT scan. Microscopic examination of the eye revealed a globe rupture with tear in the sclera, a prolapsed ciliary body, and profusely bleeding. The patient underwent emergency evisceration and remained stable post-operatively. He progressed well and was discharged after 2 weeks. Follow-up was advised.

The patient, a 68-year-old man with a history of aortic insufficiency and ascending aort dilatation, was admitted to the emergency department with exertional dyspnea and coughing. A blood pressure of 100/50 mmHg was noted, with a heart rate of 80 beats/min. A 3/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur was heard along the left sternal border, and ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Chest X-ray revealed increased cardiothoracic index and a prominent aortic arch. However, while awaiting laboratory results, the patient experienced severe chest pain, which was followed by a repeat ECG showing ST segment elevation in aVR lead and diffuse ST segment depressions in all other leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe aortic regurgitation, a dilated ascending aorta with a diameter of 5.27 cm, and intimal dissection flap that was prolapsing into the left ventricle during diastole. Left ventricular ejection fraction was within normal limits. The patient was immediately suggested surgery, but he died suddenly after CPR.

The patient, a 53-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary emphysema and recurrent pneumothorax, presented with fever, bilateral calf pain, and a cutaneous eruption over the lower extremities. She was treated for a pulmonary infection two weeks prior with Cefpodoxime. Admission blood tests showed elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin levels, and low albumin, along with a thoracic CT scan revealing a right-sided apical lesion, mediastinal, and hilar adenomegaly. Post-bronchoscopy sputum was positive for Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis was leukocytoclastic vasculitis consistent with HSP, confirmed by skin biopsy and immunofluorescence. A pulmonary aspiration smear was positive for acid-fast bacilli and sputum culture for Mycobacterium xenopi. The patient was initially treated with Colchicin 1 mg, but developed severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day was administered, along with antibiotics (Piperacillin/Tazobactam and Oxacillin), and anti-mycotic agents. Follow-up showed improvement in pulmonary lesions and no recurrence, with no renal disease found. The patient responded favorably to treatment, and no further complications were noted.
